'''''Lamium hybridum''''', the '''cut-leaved dead-nettle''',<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Cut-leaved Dead-nettle ''Lamium hybridum'' Vill. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.8rw |access-date=21 July 2024 }}</ref> is a species of ''[[Lamium]]'' native to western and northern [[Europe]] and northwestern [[Africa]].<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |author-link1=Plants of the World Online |id=448866-1 |title=''Lamium hybridum'' Vill. |access-date=21 July 2024 }}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|specific name]] means '[[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]'; however, [[Dominique Villars]], in describing the species, did not give his reasons for selecting this name. The English name refers to the deeply cut leaves, unlike the shallower lobes of other related species of ''Lamium''.

==Taxonomy==
Dominique Villars first described it as a species in 1786 in volume 1, p. 251, of his ''Histoire des Plantes de Dauphiné'',<ref name="Villars1">{{cite web |last1=Villars |first1=Dominique |title=Histoire des plantes du Dauphiné 1: 251 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/50324293 |website=BHL |date=1786 |access-date=2024-07-24}}</ref> but a year later in volume 2, p. 385, he had second thoughts about it, and reduced it to a [[variety (botany)|variety]] of the similar red dead-nettle ''[[Lamium purpureum]]''.<ref name="Villars2">{{cite web |last1=Villars |first1=Dominique |title=Histoire des plantes du Dauphiné 2: 385 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/50314700 |website=BHL |date=1787 |access-date=2024-07-24}}</ref> It was for long so treated, but recently, genetic evidence has shown it is genetically distinct from ''L. purpureum'' and should stand as a distinct species.<ref name="Taxon">{{cite journal |last1=Bendiksby |first1=Mika |last2=Brysting |first2=Anne K. |last3=Thorbek |first3=Lisbeth |last4=Gussarova |first4=Galina |last5=Ryding |first5=Olof |title=Molecular phylogeny and taxonomy of the genus ''Lamium'' L. (Lamiaceae): Disentangling origins of presumed allotetraploids |journal=Taxon |date=2011 |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=986–1000 |doi=10.1002/tax.604004 |bibcode=2011Taxon..60..986B |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266655362 |access-date=2024-07-24}}</ref> This has been accepted by ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''.<ref name="POWO"/> More interesting is the suggestion that it may indeed be of hybrid origin between ''Lamium purpureum'' and ''[[Lamium bifidum]]'',<ref name="Taxon"/> so Villars had unexpected insight in his name choice.

==Description==
[[File:Cut-leaved Dead-nettle, Liverpool, England 2.jpg|thumb|left|Cut-leaved dead-nettle in [[Liverpool]]; note the deeply incised leaves.]]
It is a low-growing [[annual plant]] growing to {{convert|10–40|cm|abbr=on}} tall, pubescent with soft, finely hairy stems. The [[leaf|leaves]] are opposite, rounded to kidney-shaped, {{convert|2–3|cm|abbr=on}} diameter, with a deeply lobed to incised margin. The [[flower]]s are a similar pink to purple colour to ''L. purpureum'', relatively small, {{convert|10–15|mm|abbr=on}} long, and form a few-flowered terminal spike with axillary whorls. The calyx is regular with five lobes and closes up after flowering. The [[Petal|corolla]] is purplish-red, fused into a short tube; the upper lip is convex, and the lower lip has three lobes, two small side ones and a larger central long one. The base of the corolla is nearly hairless, unlike ''L. purpureum'' where it is obviously ringed with hairs. There are four stamens, two long and two short. It flowers from early spring through the summer until mid autumn, typically March to October in Britain. The [[gynoecium]] has two fused carpels and the fruit is a four-chambered [[schizocarp]]. It propagates by [[seed]]. It is a [[nectar]] and [[pollen]] source for [[bee]]s.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref> 

==Distribution and habitat==
Cut-leaf dead-nettle is native to western and northern Europe, and northwest Africa in the [[Atlas Mountains]].<ref name="POWO"/> Its status in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]] is disputed; some sources give it as native,<ref name=blamey/><ref name="Swan">{{cite book |last1=Swan |first1=George A. |title=Flora of Northumberland |date=1993 |publisher=Natural History Society of Northumbria |location=Hancock Museum |isbn=0-9520782-0-1 |page=205 }}</ref> while others cite it as an [[archaeophyte]].<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/><ref name="POWO"/> It is found growing in open areas, gardens, fields and meadows, and widely in uncultivated areas in urban habitats.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/>
